summary: A 1979 note on how to address mail to hosts that are outside the network, including the form of such out-of-net addresses. Its status is unknown.

eli5.summary: How do you write the address of someone on a different network? This note suggests a way.

questions: out of net host addresses for mail
how to address mail to other networks
subtitle: How to address mail to hosts on networks other than the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: As the ARPANET began to connect with other networks, there was no standard way to address mail to users on those external networks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 754 evaluates four proposed addressing schemes: single mailbox, global names inside, global names outside, and structured names.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends structured names (Solution D), where external users are addressed with a network prefix and username, requiring minimal changes to existing software.

today: RFC 754's structured naming approach influenced mail addressing standards, but the eventual adoption of the Domain Name System (DNS) and SMTP provided a more comprehensive solution for internet-wide mail routing.

sections.title: Connecting to Other Networks
sections.content:
By 1979, interest was growing in extending the ARPANET message system to reach other computer networks, including NSW (New South Wales) and other network environments. However, the existing ARPANET mail addressing scheme did not support sending messages to users outside the ARPANET. The RFC considers four different strategies for how to encode addresses to foreign networks.

Each strategy involves trade-offs between the burden placed on mail composition programs, mail reading programs, the mail delivery daemon, and the namespace constraints of each solution.
sections.eli5: We need a way to send mail between different networks. Should the person sending the mail help figure out the address, or the person receiving it, or the mail server?

sections.title: Four Proposed Solutions
sections.content: Solution A (Single Mailbox) routes all foreign network mail to one forwarding host mailbox and uses new header lines to identify the actual recipient. Solution B (Global Names Inside) sends to a single forwarding mailbox but uses existing header fields to route the message. Solution C (Global Names Outside) sends to individual per-user mailboxes on a forwarding host, treating external users like local users. Solution D (Structured Names) creates unique per-user mailbox names with a common network prefix, like NSW-Joe or NSW-Fred, allowing the FTP server to route based on the prefix without knowing all individual users.
sections.eli5: A: One mailbox for all foreign mail, use new labels. B: One mailbox, use existing labels. C: One mailbox per person, but hard to manage. D: Mailbox name shows the network and person, like 'NSW-Joe'.

sections.title: The Recommended Approach
sections.content: Solution D is recommended because it requires the fewest changes to existing software. Only the FTP server at the forwarding host needs modification to recognize and route messages by the network prefix. No changes are needed to mail composition or reading programs. The approach uses only outside information from the mailbox argument, avoiding the syntactic and semantic problems that arise when relying on message header contents. The structured name format NSW-Joe@FWDR clearly separates the network from the user, making it self-documenting.
sections.eli5: Solution D wins because adding a name like 'NSW-' in front tells the mail server where to send it, without changing everything else.
